meta.title: Section IV — Change in the Modern World
meta.range: Apartheid in South Africa, 1960–1994 · Short answer & extended response, 25 marks, ~45 min

boxes.label: Examinable
boxes.bodyHtml: The ideology and legislative machinery of the apartheid state, Sharpeville and its aftermath, the Black Consciousness Movement, the Soweto Uprising, and internal resistance movements (trade unions, UDF, student and civic organisations, women's resistance).

boxes.label: Excluded
boxes.bodyHtml:
• Mandela as Head of the ANC
  • Tactics of repression / SA security forces
  • Bantustans & independent black states
  • Relations with neighbouring African countries
  • International responses to apartheid
  • The end of apartheid & transition to democracy

summary.note: Every official syllabus dot point for this topic is listed below, grouped as the syllabus itself groups them.

groups.title: Survey — The Nature of the Apartheid System
points: Political, economic, social and demographic issues in South Africa in 1960: the Population Registration Act (1950) required racial classification; growing internal dissent met increasing white anxiety and calls for tougher laws; rapid African decolonisation post-WWII left white-minority rule internationally isolated.

Apartheid: ideology, policy and practice: built on the pseudo-scientific claim that races needed separation for "mutual benefit"; enforced through legislation including the Group Areas Act (1950), Pass Laws Act (1952), Bantu Education Act (1953) and Reservation of Separate Amenities Act (1953).

Impact of apartheid on rural and urban communities: forced removals (e.g. an estimated 60,000 residents removed from Sophiatown to Soweto from 1955), township overcrowding, and severely under-resourced services for Black South Africans compared with whites.

groups.title: National Resistance to Apartheid
points: The nature, growth and impact of the ANC and the PAC: ANC founded 1912, adopted the Programme of Action (1949) and Freedom Charter (1955); PAC split from the ANC in 1959 under Robert Sobukwe, favouring a more explicitly Africanist platform.

Significance of the Sharpeville Massacre: on 21 March 1960, police killed at least 69 and wounded around 186 protesters at a PAC-organised anti-pass demonstration, leading to a State of Emergency and the banning of the ANC and PAC.

Mandela as head of Umkhonto we Sizwe ("The Spear of the Nation", MK): after the 1960 bannings, Mandela helped establish the ANC's armed wing in 1961, coordinating sabotage attacks on infrastructure before his arrest in 1962.

Rivonia Trial, imprisonment on Robben Island, the Free Mandela campaign: senior MK leaders were arrested in 1963; Mandela was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964 and held on Robben Island, becoming an international symbol of resistance.

Role of Mandela's leadership of the ANC: as leader of the ANC Youth League from the late 1940s, Mandela helped push the ANC toward mass action; his legal career as part of South Africa's first Black law firm gave him a close view of apartheid's daily impact and shaped his turn toward MK's sabotage campaign in 1961. Imprisoned from 1962, he became the living symbol of the "Free Mandela" campaign — his refusal of a conditional release in the 1980s ("only free men can negotiate... your freedom and mine cannot be separated") kept his moral authority intact. After his 1990 release he proved a skilled negotiator, signing the Groote Schuur Minute (May 1990) and National Peace Accord (Sept 1990) with the National Party and Inkatha, publicly renouncing violence, and steering the ANC through the CODESA talks toward the 1994 election — historians credit his leadership as decisive in preventing the transition from collapsing into civil war.

Significance of Steve Biko and the Black Consciousness Movement: SASO founded by Biko and others (1968–69), the Black People's Convention formed 1972; Biko died in police detention on 12 September 1977.

groups.title: Resistance to Apartheid — The Soweto Uprising & Internal Resistance, 1970s–1980s
points: The Soweto Uprising, 16 June 1976: triggered by a 1974 decree mandating Afrikaans as a medium of instruction, layered on decades of Bantu Education underfunding; deaths in the unrest that followed range from an official figure of around 176 to independent estimates of over 600.

Trade unions: the Durban strikes of 1973 (around 100,000 workers) demonstrated organised economic leverage; the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) formed in 1985 with roughly 500,000 initial members.

The United Democratic Front (UDF): launched 1983 to oppose the tricameral constitution, uniting an estimated 400-plus civic, student, church and union organisations into a coordinated national movement before being effectively banned in 1988.

Women's resistance: the Federation of South African Women (founded 1954) organised the 20,000-strong march on the Union Buildings on 9 August 1956; women's community networks sustained township-based campaigns through the 1970s–80s.

Student and civic organisations: school boycotts and bodies such as the Congress of South African Students (COSAS, founded 1979) kept education-related grievances active, with many organisations affiliating with the UDF from 1983.

groups.title: Repression and Control by South African Governments
points: Legal tactics of repression: the Suppression of Communism Act (1950) defined "communism" broadly enough to ban almost any resistance or criticism of the government; the Public Safety Act (1953) let the government declare a renewable 12-month State of Emergency; the General Law Amendment Act (1963) let police detain suspects for 90 days without charge or legal access, extendable indefinitely at the Minister of Justice's discretion, with the courts unable to intervene; the Terrorism Act (1967) allowed the death penalty for a broad range of offences.

"Total Strategy" under Botha: facing slowing growth and rising unrest in the 1970s, P.W. Botha framed resistance as a "total onslaught" requiring a "Total National Strategy" combining limited social reforms (easing pass laws, recognising Black trade unions, repealing the Mixed Marriages Act) with the 1983 Tricameral Parliament (separate white, Coloured and Indian chambers that still excluded Black South Africans entirely) and greatly expanded military and police powers.

Role of South African security forces: the merged police and South African Defence Force (SADF), alongside secret bodies like the Bureau of State Security (BOSS), used mass detention without charge (around 30,000 people detained by 1988), police brutality and deaths in custody (including Steve Biko's 1977 death), and covert units such as Koevoet and "kitskonstable" vigilantes accused of torture and extrajudicial killing; the SADF also carried out over 40 assassinations and cross-border raids into neighbouring states. Military spending rose from R72 million (1961) to R3 billion (1981), and sequential States of Emergency from 1985 gave the security apparatus sweeping, largely unaccountable power.

Role and significance of Bantustans and independent "black states": ten ethnically defined "homelands" (Transkei, Bophuthatswana, Venda, Ciskei and six others) confined Black South Africans to about 13% of the land; the 1970 Black Homelands Citizenship Act stripped Black South Africans of South African citizenship, reassigning it to a Bantustan regardless of where they actually lived or worked. From 1976 four Bantustans (Transkei, Bophuthatswana, Venda, Ciskei) were granted nominal "independence", but none were recognised by any country besides South Africa itself, none were economically self-sufficient, and their appointed chiefs were widely seen as apartheid's proxies — the policy's deeper aim was to fragment Black South Africans into separate ethnic "nations" and so undercut a unified national resistance movement.

Relations with neighbouring African countries: as Portugal's African colonies (Angola, Mozambique) and British-ruled territories in the region won independence through the 1960s–70s, South Africa saw a hostile, decolonising "frontline" forming around it, providing bases for exiled ANC/MK fighters. Under Botha's "Policy of Forward Defence", the SADF conducted cross-border raids and backed anti-communist insurgencies — supporting UNITA against the Marxist MPLA government in Angola, and RENAMO against FRELIMO in Mozambique (despite signing the 1984 Nkomati Accord promising to stop, which South Africa did not honour) — while also fighting a long, costly war to retain control of South West Africa (Namibia) against SWAPO insurgents until finally conceding Namibian independence in 1990.

International responses to South African policies: the UN General Assembly condemned apartheid from the 1950s and formally called for its end after Sharpeville (1960), later imposing a voluntary (1963) then mandatory (1977) arms embargo; South Africa was suspended from the UN in 1974. The Commonwealth (Gleneagles Agreement, 1977) and sporting bodies excluded South African teams from the Olympics (1964), FIFA (1963) and international cricket and rugby for most of the period, while the Anti-Apartheid Movement organised sustained public campaigns — including a 1988 Wembley concert marking Mandela's 70th birthday, watched by an estimated 600 million people worldwide. The UK and US under Thatcher and Reagan initially resisted mandatory sanctions on Cold War and free-market grounds, but grassroots consumer boycotts and disinvestment campaigns still drove US firms and international banks to withdraw heavily from South Africa through the 1980s.

groups.title: End of Apartheid
points: Political factors: the 1983 Tricameral Parliament, which still excluded Black South Africans entirely, triggered mass mobilisation through bodies like the United Democratic Front (est. 1983, over 1,000 affiliated organisations) and the trade union federation COSATU (est. 1985, 500,000+ members), whose strikes and boycotts pursued the ANC's aim to "make apartheid unworkable, make the country ungovernable"; sustained township unrest and Botha's escalating States of Emergency (from 1985) fed a cycle of violence and repression that convinced even factions within the ruling National Party — which itself splintered between hardline (Conservative Party, AWB) and reformist wings — that the status quo was unsustainable.

Economic factors: historians widely regard the economic collapse as the most decisive cause — mounting international sanctions and disinvestment (roughly 40% of US investment withdrawn within four years of 1986 US sanctions), a 50% fall in gold prices, a 1985 debt crisis that forced the temporary closure of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, and spiralling military spending together pushed economic growth to around 1.5% by early 1989, directly eroding white South Africans' economic confidence in apartheid's viability.

Social factors: deepening Black poverty, worsened by the loss of South African citizenship under the 1970 Black Homelands Citizenship Act, fed growing unrest, youth radicalisation ("Liberation before Education") and alternative community structures (people's courts, street committees); violence increasingly turned inward too, including the punishment tactic of "necklacing" against suspected collaborators and escalating clashes between the ANC and the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party.

International factors: sustained global sanctions, sporting and cultural boycotts, and diplomatic isolation (detailed under International Responses above) combined with the economic factors to leave South Africa financially isolated by the late 1980s; the end of the Cold War and the collapse of Soviet-backed communism by 1989 also removed the National Party's central ideological justification for resisting Black majority rule — de Klerk himself no longer saw the ANC's historic ties to the SACP as a serious external threat, clearing the way for his 2 February 1990 speech unbanning the ANC, PAC and SACP and releasing political prisoners including Mandela.

sources.tag: Source C — Adapted eyewitness recollection, Soweto, June 1976 (composite, for practice use)
sources.bodyHtml: "We were walking from Orlando West to join the other schools, carrying our placards about Afrikaans in the classroom. None of us expected police vehicles to be waiting at the intersection. When the first shots rang out, students scattered, but by the afternoon the crowds had reformed — angrier, and no longer just about the language issue."

sources.tag: Source O — Photograph, a family awaiting relocation from Sophiatown, 1955
sources.bodyHtml: A family sits with their possessions — a mattress, a basin, bundled belongings — in front of a partly demolished house, waiting to be relocated. Removals from Sophiatown, one of the few areas where Black South Africans could own land, began on 9 February 1955 under the Natives Resettlement Act (1954); the area was later rebuilt as a white suburb renamed Triomf.

sources.tag: Source P — Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom, 2013 edition, p. 118
sources.bodyHtml: "Mass action was perilous in South Africa, where it was a criminal offence to strike, and where the rights of free speech and movement were unmercifully curtailed. By striking, an African worker stood to not only lose his job but his entire livelihood and the right to stay in the area he was living."

sources.tag: Source Q — Eyewitness testimonies from Sharpeville, quoted in Tom Lodge, Sharpeville: An Apartheid Massacre and its Consequences, 2011, pp. 12–13
sources.bodyHtml:
Testimony of eyewitness Carlton Monnakgotla: "I stood frozen, couldn't believe what was happening. Then I saw the bodies and people fleeing. Right in front of me a pregnant woman was shot. Her unborn baby fell out of her stomach and the next bullet got her. Horrible."
Testimony of eyewitness Ruben Rapoetsoe: "[W]hen I passed the police station again I heard officers shouting: 'Where is your land now, kaffirs? Where is your land now?' … During the shooting, there was a man who, despite the bullets, ran straight towards the police station, shouting: 'It's enough, you've shot enough!' He was shot moments later."

sources.tag: Source R — A Free Nelson Mandela Campaign poster, 1988, published by The Pyramid Complex, Washington D.C.
sources.bodyHtml: Mandela's face is imposed onto a map of Africa, beneath the words "Must Be Set Free!!!" in bold red text — the demand for his release presented as a cause for the whole continent, not South Africa alone.

sources.tag: Source S — Peter Gabriel, 'Biko', 1980 — a musical eulogy and anti-apartheid song
sources.bodyHtml: "September '77 / Port Elizabeth weather fine / It was business as usual / In police room 619 … Yihla Moja, Yihla Moja — the man is dead … You can blow out a candle / But you can't blow out a fire / Once the flames begin to catch / The wind will blow it higher … And the eyes of the world are watching now." ('Yihla Moja' is Xhosa for 'come spirit'.)

sources.tag: Source T — Truth and Reconciliation Commission, 'The Former South African Government and its Security Forces', 1998
sources.bodyHtml: "The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (the Commission) found the state — and in particular its security agencies and affiliated policy and strategy formulation committees and councils — to be the primary perpetrators of gross violations of human rights committed during the thirty-four years it was mandated to investigate [1960–94]."

sources.tag: Source U — Photograph, a young boy at an AWB rally, Rustenburg, 1994
sources.bodyHtml: A young boy prays during a rally of the Afrikaner Weerstandsbeweging (AWB). The flag behind him carries the AWB's three-sevens emblem, deliberately styled on the Nazi swastika.

sources.tag: Source V — Nelson Mandela on South African military incursions
sources.bodyHtml: "In 1981, the South African Defence Force launched a raid on ANC offices in Maputo, Mozambique, killing thirteen of our people, including women and children. In December 1982 … the South African military again attacked an ANC outpost in Maseru, Lesotho, killing forty-two people, including a dozen women and children."

groups.title: Origins & Ideology of the Apartheid State

questions.questionHtml: Explain the ideology behind apartheid and how the National Party used it to win and consolidate power after 1948.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. 1948 election: D.F. Malan's National Party won on an explicit platform of "apartheid" (Afrikaans for "apartness"), narrowly defeating Smuts' United Party.
  2. Core ideology: a hierarchy of races with whites at the top, justified through claims of "separate development" — that each race should develop within its own areas, institutions and culture rather than compete within one society.
  3. From theory to law: apartheid marked a deliberate escalation from the informal segregation of 1910–1948 to a comprehensive legal system enforced through dedicated legislation and a purpose-built bureaucracy.
  4. "Grand apartheid": under Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd from 1958, the ideology extended to the idea of separate "homelands" as the supposed political fulfilment of separate development.
Historian's view — verified quote
Political scientist Gwendolen Carter, who studied the implementation of apartheid in South Africa in the early 1950s, argued the National Party government was intent on using legislative action "to make the African the different kind of person that theory [apartheid] says he is."Gwendolen Carter, The Politics of Inequality (1958), pp. 15, 411–12, cited in Clark & Worger, South Africa: The Rise and Fall of Apartheid (2011)
Useful for arguing apartheid was not just inherited prejudice but an actively engineered, forward-looking legal project — theory driving policy, not simply describing existing practice.

groups.title: Source-Based & the Machinery of the Apartheid State

questions.questionHtml: According to Source C, how did the mood of the protest change over the course of 16 June 1976?
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include
  • Begins as an organised, focused protest specifically about the use of Afrikaans in schools.
  • Shifts after police shootings — anger broadens beyond the original language grievance.
  • Quote or paraphrase the detail that crowds "reformed" rather than dispersing, showing resolve rather than intimidation.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the key features of apartheid legislation (e.g. the Population Registration Act and the Group Areas Act) and their impact on daily life for Black South Africans.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Population Registration Act (1950): classified every citizen into a racial category (White, Coloured, Indian, African/Bantu), forming the legal basis for all other apartheid laws.
  2. Group Areas Act (1950): designated separate residential and business areas by race, enabling forced removals from mixed or "white" areas — e.g. an estimated 60,000 residents were removed from Sophiatown to Soweto from 1955.
  3. Pass laws: the 1952 Natives (Abolition of Passes and Co-ordination of Documents) Act required every Black South African over 16 to carry a "reference book" (dompas) at all times, controlling movement into urban/"white" areas.
  4. Cumulative impact: entrenched economic disadvantage, broke up families and communities, and formalised segregation in nearly every part of daily life.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the purpose and impact of the Bantu Education Act (1953) on Black South African communities.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Purpose: deliberately limited curriculum and funding, with Verwoerd (then Minister for Native Affairs) stating Africans should be educated for a subordinate role in the economy rather than academic advancement.
  • Impact: government spending per Black pupil remained a small fraction of spending per white pupil throughout the 1950s–60s, producing chronic overcrowding and under-resourced classrooms.
  • Link forward: this resentment — compounded by a 1974 decree requiring certain subjects to be taught via Afrikaans — is the direct background to the 1976 Soweto Uprising.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the causes and immediate consequences of the Sharpeville massacre of 21 March 1960.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Cause: a PAC-organised protest against pass laws, in which crowds gathered at the Sharpeville police station on 21 March 1960 offering themselves for arrest without their passes.
  2. The event: police opened fire on the crowd, killing at least 69 people and wounding around 186 — many shot in the back as they fled.
  3. Consequence — domestic: the government declared a State of Emergency and banned both the ANC and PAC shortly afterward under the Unlawful Organizations Act (April 1960).
  4. Consequence — strategic: pushed resistance movements toward the view that non-violent protest alone was insufficient — both organisations formed armed wings (the ANC's Umkhonto we Sizwe and the PAC's Poqo) by 1961.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the impact of the banning of the ANC and PAC in 1960 on the strategies used by anti-apartheid movements over the following decade.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Immediate effect: organisations forced underground or into exile; senior leaders including Nelson Mandela were sentenced to life imprisonment at the Rivonia Trial (1963–64), disrupting internal leadership networks.
  2. Strategic shift: a move by some toward more radical, clandestine resistance rather than open mass organising, given the risk of banning and arrest.
  3. Vacuum: the resulting gap in visible internal leadership through the 1960s created space for a new kind of movement to emerge later in the decade.
  4. Link forward: this vacuum helps explain why the Black Consciousness Movement, built by a new generation of students from 1968–69, was able to develop a distinct, independent voice by the early 1970s.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the significance of the Black Consciousness Movement, including the role of Steve Biko, in shaping resistance to apartheid during the 1970s.
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

The Black Consciousness Movement's most significant contribution was not any immediate policy concession it won from the apartheid state, but the psychological and organisational reshaping of resistance it achieved — a shift that directly prepared the generation of students who drove the Soweto Uprising the following decade.

Body Paragraph 1 — core ideas

Black Consciousness deliberately rejected the white-led, liberal opposition model that had previously dominated anti-apartheid politics, arguing instead for Black pride and self-reliance as the necessary starting point for resistance. It treated Africans, Coloureds and Indians as a single shared "Black" political identity, consciously uniting groups apartheid legislation had gone to great administrative lengths to keep legally and socially separate — a direct ideological challenge to the racial categorisation the Population Registration Act had imposed since 1950. Central to this was the movement's emphasis on psychological liberation from apartheid's dehumanising ideology as a precondition for effective political action, on the reasoning that a population conditioned to see itself as inferior could not organise effective resistance until that internal conditioning was broken.

Body Paragraph 2 — organisational significance

This ideology translated into a genuinely independent institutional base rather than remaining abstract rhetoric. The South African Students' Organisation, founded by Biko and others in 1968–69, broke deliberately from the multiracial National Union of South African Students, on the grounds that a movement led even partly by white liberals could not fully embody Black self-reliance. The Black People's Convention, formed in 1972, extended this organisational model beyond university campuses into a wider community structure — evidence that Black Consciousness was building durable institutions, not simply articulating a philosophy confined to student politics.

Body Paragraph 3 — the link to 1976 and its aftermath

The movement's ideas fed directly into the generation that organised the Soweto protests, and its subsequent suppression only reinforced its significance. SASO was banned in 1977, and Biko himself died in police detention on 12 September 1977 after being arrested under the Terrorism Act — his death, rather than silencing the movement's ideas, drew substantial international attention to them and to the apartheid state's methods of repression more broadly.

Conclusion — Judgement

Black Consciousness's significance lies less in any immediate legislative change than in how thoroughly it reshaped a generation's understanding of resistance and identity — a legacy that outlasted Biko's death and fed directly into the mass, youth-led movements that followed through the late 1970s and 1980s.

Primary source — verified quote
"The most potent weapon in the hands of the oppressor is the mind of the oppressed."Steve Biko, "White Racism and Black Consciousness" (1971), in I Write What I Like (1978)
Biko's own words are the clearest possible evidence of what Black Consciousness was actually arguing — that liberation had to begin with a psychological break from apartheid's assumptions before it could become a political movement.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the significance of the Soweto Uprising of 1976 as a turning point in the resistance to apartheid.
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

Soweto marked a genuine turning point in the resistance to apartheid because it shifted the locus of opposition from adult-led, formal organisations to a mass, youth-driven movement whose momentum proved national in scale and lasting in effect.

Body Paragraph 1 — the immediate trigger

The immediate spark was administrative but landed on ground already primed for revolt: a 1974 decree requiring Afrikaans as the medium of instruction for certain subjects was layered on top of decades of chronic Bantu Education underfunding, meaning the language decree functioned less as an isolated grievance than as the final, unbearable addition to a much longer accumulation of educational disadvantage.

Body Paragraph 2 — the scale of the event

What followed escalated far beyond what the language issue alone would suggest. A student march on 16 June 1976 was met with police gunfire, and the resulting unrest spread rapidly from Soweto to townships across the country over the following months rather than remaining a localised, contained incident. Estimates of deaths in the unrest that followed range from an official government figure of around 176 up to independent estimates of over 600 — a gap between official and independent counts that itself indicates the scale of state violence involved and the state's incentive to understate it.

Body Paragraph 3 — short- and longer-term significance

The uprising's consequences extended well beyond 1976 itself. Thousands of young people fled into exile, many joining the ANC's armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, directly linking the uprising to the growth of armed resistance abroad. Domestically, the uprising re-energised both internal and international attention on apartheid and produced a new generation of politicised activists who went on to shape resistance through the 1980s, including many who later became organisers within the UDF.

Conclusion — Judgement

Soweto did not end apartheid, but it permanently changed who led the resistance to it: from 1976 onward, young people and mass mobilisation, rather than formal political organisations alone, drove the movement forward — a structural shift in leadership, not merely a single dramatic episode.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the role of trade unions in internal resistance to apartheid during the 1970s and 1980s.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Background: the Durban strikes of 1973, involving an estimated 100,000 Black workers, demonstrated organised economic leverage even while political parties remained banned.
  2. Growth: formation of independent Black trade unions through the 1970s, culminating in the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), formed 1985 with an initial membership of around 500,000 workers.
  3. Significance: linked economic grievances to the wider political struggle, and gave ordinary workers — not just students or intellectuals — an organised, legally harder-to-ban role in resistance.

questions.questionHtml: To what extent did the formation of the United Democratic Front (UDF) in 1983 change the nature of internal resistance to apartheid?
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

The formation of the United Democratic Front marked a decisive structural shift in internal resistance to apartheid, from fragmented, localised action to a genuinely national, mass-based opposition movement — a change in the nature of resistance, not merely its scale.

Body Paragraph 1 — the circumstances of formation

The UDF was launched in 1983 specifically to oppose the government's new tricameral constitution, which offered limited parliamentary representation to Coloured and Indian communities while excluding Africans entirely — a reform transparently designed to divide opposition along racial lines rather than address the underlying demand for full political rights. In direct response, the UDF united an estimated 400-plus civic, student, church and union organisations into a single coordinated umbrella body, a scale of coalition-building without precedent in the internal resistance movement since the ANC and PAC were banned in 1960.

Body Paragraph 2 — the new scale of coordinated action

This coalition structure translated directly into a new operational capacity. The UDF enabled genuinely nationwide, coordinated campaigns — rent and consumer boycotts, township-based civic action, stayaways — at a scale that had simply not been organisationally possible while resistance remained fragmented across hundreds of separate local bodies, and it achieved this despite the ANC and PAC themselves remaining banned throughout the period.

Body Paragraph 3 — the breadth of its social base

The UDF also drew in a far wider cross-section of society than earlier resistance movements had managed, incorporating students, workers, clergy and women's organisations under one loosely federated, explicitly multiracial structure. This breadth sustained the movement for five years until it was effectively banned from operating, alongside COSATU, in 1988 — evidence that the state itself judged the UDF's coalition model to be a serious enough threat to warrant the same repressive measures previously reserved for the ANC and PAC.

Conclusion — Judgement

The UDF's scale and coordination gave internal resistance a genuinely national character for the first time since the ANC and PAC were banned in 1960 — a structural transformation in how resistance was organised, confirmed by the fact that the apartheid state ultimately treated it as seriously enough of a threat to ban.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the role of women in resistance to apartheid.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • The Federation of South African Women, founded 1954, organised the march of an estimated 20,000 women on the Union Buildings in Pretoria on 9 August 1956 to protest pass laws.
  • Central role in sustaining township-based campaigns from the 1970s–80s — rent boycotts, consumer boycotts, and local civic organisation — which depended heavily on women's community networks.
  • Often bore the practical burden of resistance while men were detained, in exile, or working migrant labour, making women's organising essential to the movement's continuity throughout the UDF era.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the role of student and civic organisations in sustaining resistance to apartheid during the 1980s.
questions.planHtml:
Structure & evidence
  1. Student organisation: school boycotts and student representative structures kept education-related grievances active a decade on from Soweto, feeding into bodies such as the Congress of South African Students (COSAS, founded 1979).
  2. Civic organisations: township-based civic associations organised around local issues — rent, services, transport — turning everyday grievances into sustained collective action.
  3. Coordination: many of these bodies affiliated with the UDF from 1983, giving local activism a national political dimension and enabling coordinated national campaigns rather than isolated local protests.

groups.title: Section IV Source Set — Sources O–V

questions.questionHtml: Describe the differing visions of democracy held by the National Party and the African National Congress.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Afrikaner Nationalists framed apartheid as a divinely sanctioned duty, reinforced by the Dutch Reformed Church and by 'scientific racism' — democracy defined by race rather than by the whole population.
  • The Native Representation Act (1936) removed Africans from the common voters' roll entirely, and the 1983 Tricameral Parliament allocated 178 seats to whites, 85 to Coloureds and 45 to Indians, with none for Africans — the National Party's vision put into practice.
  • Verwoerd, addressing London in 1961: "We do not only want to ensure white survival. We seek a solution which will ensure survival and full development... to each of the other racial groups" — separate development presented as democracy, not its denial.
  • The ANC, formed in 1912, campaigned for a single non-racial democracy; the Freedom Charter (1955) declared "The people shall govern... All national groups shall have equal rights... All shall be equal before the law."
  • Mandela, 1964: "I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination" — rejecting both minority rule and majority tyranny, in contrast to Sobukwe's PAC, which called for "Government of the Africans by the Africans and for the Africans."

questions.questionHtml: Describe the methods of repression used by the South African government to control opposition.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Legal repression: the Suppression of Communism Act (1950) allowed any resistance to be classified as communism, and the General Law Amendment Act (1963) permitted 90 days' detention without charge or a lawyer, repeatable indefinitely.
  • Physical repression: military personnel grew from 106,000 in 1961 to 592,000 in 1981, and around 30,000 people had been detained by 1988; units such as Koevoet received bounty payments for killing suspected guerrillas.
  • Control of information: the Protection of Information Act meant an arrest could not be reported unless the press could prove it endangered no state security, and the newspaper The World was closed in 1977.
  • Everyday control: pass laws produced up to 500,000 arrests each year, and the Bantustan system divided Africans along ethnic lines to weaken a unified African identity.
  • Historians Clark and Worger judged that the legal system vested so many powers in the police rather than the courts that the country "operated for most of its inhabitants as a police state."

questions.questionHtml: Describe the changes in South African society between 1960 and 1994.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Where people lived: the homelands' share of the population rose from 39% (4.4 million) in 1960 to 53% (11 million) in 1980, though only around one third of Black South Africans ever actually lived in the Bantustans.
  • Who organised: trade unions were recognised under Total Strategy, and COSATU reached 500,000 members, with over 1 million workdays lost to strikes in 1986; authority also moved into township hands through people's courts and street committees.
  • White society fractured: the Herstigte Nasionale Party broke away in 1968, and by 1987 the Conservative Party won 26% of the vote and 37% of the Afrikaner vote.
  • The law was dismantled rapidly at the end: the ANC, PAC and SACP were unbanned and the Separate Amenities Act repealed in 1990, and the Group Areas Act followed in 1991; the April 1994 election drew 91% turnout.
  • But social structure outlived the laws: the bottom 40% of the population still earned only 6% of national income after apartheid ended.

questions.questionHtml: With reference to Source O and your own knowledge, explain the impact of forced removals on Black South African communities.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Source O shows a family and their possessions in front of a gutted house — the domestic scale of forced removal, made visible at the level of one household rather than described only in hectares or percentages.
  • Sophiatown was one of the few areas where Black South Africans could own land; removals began on 9 February 1955 under the Natives Resettlement Act (1954), and the area was rebuilt as a white suburb renamed Triomf.
  • The policy rested on the Natives Land Act (1913), which restricted Africans to 8% of the country (raised to 13% in 1936), and the Group Areas Act (1950), which redrew urban boundaries around racial lines.
  • The homelands' population grew from 4.4 million (39%) in 1960 to 11 million (53%) in 1980, with population densities of up to 298 per square kilometre in areas with poor soil and minimal infrastructure.
  • The Black Homelands Citizenship Act (1970) revoked South African citizenship for people assigned to a homeland, and infant mortality was around thirteen times higher for African and Coloured children than for white children.
  • Source O dates from 1955, at the very start of the period under investigation — of high value for illustrating the human scale of removals, though it should be read alongside evidence of the policy's growth over the following decades.

questions.questionHtml: With reference to Source T and your own knowledge, explain the impact of the South African government's use of state terror.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Source T, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's 1998 report, found the state and "in particular its security agencies and affiliated policy and strategy formulation committees and councils" to be the primary perpetrators of gross human rights violations across the 34 years it investigated (1960–94) — establishing that repression was policy, not the excesses of rogue officers.
  • Impact 1 — it worked: after Sharpeville, the ANC and PAC were banned within nine days and a state of emergency allowed 11,000 detentions; Steve Biko was detained without charge for 137 days and died in custody on 12 September 1977, with no officer charged with his murder at the time.
  • Impact 2 — it was self-defeating: Mandela founded MK after Sharpeville on the basis that "violence was the only weapon that would destroy apartheid", and the Soweto Uprising of 16 June 1976, in which as many as 700 students were killed, has been described as a turning point that helped end apartheid.
  • Nationwide states of emergency from 1986, which left 600 dead in their first six months, fuelled resentment rather than restoring order, and the combined cost of military spending and disinvestment meant 14% of all government spending went on debt repayments by 1988.
  • The TRC itself found over 20,000 victims of gross human rights abuse and granted amnesty to only 849 of 5,392 applicants — evidence, from the state's own post-apartheid inquiry, of both the scale of state terror and its ultimate cost.

questions.questionHtml: Using Sources Q and S, explain how the deaths of protestors and activists shaped resistance to apartheid.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Source Q, eyewitness testimony from Sharpeville, describes police continuing to fire after resistance had stopped — corroborated by the TRC's finding that protestors were acting peacefully and police "were not used to being disobeyed."
  • Sharpeville (69 killed, 180 injured) led directly to the ANC and PAC being banned and to the founding of MK in 1961 by Mandela, Sisulu and Slovo, and of the PAC's Poqo, "the first black political organisation in South Africa that openly accepted the taking of human life as part of its strategy" — the deaths ended non-violent protest as a viable strategy inside South Africa.
  • Source S, Peter Gabriel's 1980 song 'Biko', names the room of Biko's death ("In police room 619") and argues that killing an activist strengthens rather than ends a movement: "You can blow out a candle / But you can't blow out a fire."
  • Biko's death drew condemnation from the UN and the US Congress, showing that Source S's closing line — "the eyes of the world are watching now" — reflected a real change in resistance's audience, from domestic to international.
  • The two sources show resistance changing in two different ways twenty years apart: Q shows a change in method inside South Africa in 1960, while S shows a change in audience abroad by 1980 — though Source S, a song written by a British musician three years after Biko's death, is evidence of international reaction rather than of the event itself.

questions.questionHtml: With reference to Source V and your own knowledge, explain the changing nature of relations between South Africa and its neighbouring countries.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Source V, Mandela's account of South African military incursions, describes the 1981 SADF raid on ANC offices in Maputo, Mozambique (killing thirteen) and the December 1982 attack on an ANC outpost in Maseru, Lesotho (killing forty-two) — two raids twenty months apart, evidence of a standing policy rather than an isolated act.
  • Relations changed as neighbouring countries gained independence — Zambia in 1964, Botswana and Lesotho in 1966, Angola and Mozambique in 1975 — and the ANC and PAC, banned at home, began operating from these states; MK established its central headquarters in Angola in 1976.
  • Under Botha's 'Total Strategy', the SADF's policy of Forward Defence carried out cross-border raids and was responsible for over 40 assassinations, deaths and abductions outside South Africa, while South Africa also armed the Mozambique National Resistance to destabilise the Mozambican government.
  • Agreements such as the Nkomati Accord (16 March 1984), in which South Africa agreed to stop intervening in Mozambique in exchange for Mozambique ending support for the ANC, were tactical and were broken.
  • Relations changed decisively only once international sanctions made destabilisation unaffordable: South Africa recognised SWAPO as the legitimate representative of Namibia in 1988 and conceded Namibian independence in 1990, showing that economic pressure, not diplomacy, ended the policy Source V describes.

questions.questionHtml: To what extent did resistance to apartheid change between 1960 and 1994? In your answer, refer to Source P.
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

Resistance to apartheid changed almost completely in its methods, its social base and its arena of action — moving from a legalistic, urban and elite campaign to an armed, mass and international one — but its stated aim never changed at all, and that continuity of aim is what made a negotiated settlement possible in 1994.

Body Paragraph 1 — Source P and the starting point

Source P, Mandela's account in Long Walk to Freedom, explains why early resistance was cautious: mass action was "perilous in South Africa, where it was a criminal offence to strike, and where the rights of free speech and movement were unmercifully curtailed," and striking risked "not only [an African worker's] job but his entire livelihood and the right to stay in the area he was living." The ANC was at first unwilling to use mass demonstrations or violent methods, and the Defiance Campaign of 1952, which deliberately overloaded the courts by breaking pass laws, saw up to 8,000 arrests and ultimately failed — though it grew ANC membership from 7,000 to 100,000 and produced the Freedom Charter of 1955.

Body Paragraph 2 — change in methods

Sharpeville, 21 March 1960, in which 69 protestors were killed and 180 injured, was the moment legal protest effectively ceased to exist: the ANC and PAC were banned within nine days. Mandela founded MK in 1961 to sabotage government infrastructure "to convince the government that apartheid was too expensive to pursue," while the PAC's Poqo openly accepted killing as a tactic. This should be balanced against the fact that MK's attacks rose from 136 in 1985 to 228 in 1986 but "were never really a threat to the government" militarily — armed struggle mattered symbolically more than it did militarily.

Body Paragraph 3 — change in base and arena

The Soweto Uprising of 16 June 1976 involved around 20,000 school students, showing resistance had become generational and could no longer be decapitated by banning a single leadership; Biko's Black Consciousness Movement asked Black South Africans to remake their own identity after "300 years of deliberate oppression, denigration and derision." By the mid-1980s, COSATU had 500,000 members and lost over 1 million workdays to strikes in 1986, and the UDF, formed in 1983, coordinated over 1,000 affiliated organisations under Tambo's call to "make apartheid unworkable! Make the country ungovernable!" Resistance also moved abroad: the Free Mandela Campaign, launched in 1980, culminated in the Wembley concert of 11 June 1988, attended by 92,000 people and broadcast globally by the BBC, while consumer boycotts drove 250 companies out of South Africa by 1987.

Conclusion — Judgement

Despite this transformation, the Freedom Charter of 1955 was formally adopted by both the UDF and COSATU by 1987, and on his release in February 1990 Mandela repeated, almost verbatim, the words he had used at his 1964 trial: "I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination." Resistance to apartheid therefore changed almost completely in method, social base and arena of action — but not at all in its underlying aim, which is why negotiation, rather than the outright victory of one side, was ultimately possible.

questions.questionHtml: Using Sources R and U and your own knowledge, assess the problems faced by South Africa in the transition to democracy.
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

The transition's central problem is framed by the two sources at its extremes: Source R shows the weight of expectation built around Mandela over a decade of international campaigning, while Source U shows an armed white constituency that rejected the settlement outright; the transition succeeded because neither pole was allowed to destroy it, and because Mandela and de Klerk each spent their own authority restraining their own side.

Body Paragraph 1 — Source R, the problem of expectation

Source R, a 1988 Free Nelson Mandela poster published in Washington D.C., imposes Mandela's face onto a map of Africa beneath the words "Must Be Set Free!!!" — evidence of a campaign, launched by Tambo in 1980, that had grown to include a petition of 20,000 mayors' names and the Wembley concert of 11 June 1988, attended by 92,000 people. The South African government made it a crime to carry or promote Mandela's image, and Albertina Sisulu stated bluntly: "As long as the government won't release Mandela, there will be no peace in this country." Mandela himself refused early release on condition of renouncing violence, insisting "only free men can negotiate. Prisoners cannot enter into contracts" — so by 1990, expectations of his release, and of what it would deliver, were immense.

Body Paragraph 2 — Source U, the problem of rejection

Source U, a 1994 photograph of a child at an AWB rally in Rustenburg holding the movement's three-sevens flag — deliberately styled on the Nazi swastika — shows that rejection of the settlement was ideological as well as electoral, and extended to the next generation. The AWB's leader, Terre'Blanche, encouraged whites to oppose every measure de Klerk introduced and led bombing campaigns and an attempt to assassinate Mandela; the AWB was the extreme edge of a wider fracture in Afrikaner politics, evident in the Conservative Party's 26% of the vote (and 37% of the Afrikaner vote) in 1987.

Body Paragraph 3 — other problems, and how they were overcome

Political violence killed 3,600 people in 1990 alone, including 46 at Boipatong in June 1992, and negotiations at CODESA collapsed more than once over who would control the armed forces during the transition. These problems were overcome through a sequence of agreements — the Groote Schuur Minute (May 1990), the National Peace Accord (1991) and the CODESA II deal of November 1993 — and through de Klerk's March 1992 referendum, in which 68% of white voters backed continued reform, directly answering the threat shown in Source U. The settlement itself, with 400 seats decided by proportional representation and a five-year Government of National Unity guaranteed to any party winning 5% of the vote, was designed specifically to reassure the side that had lost.

Conclusion — Judgement

The April 1994 election ran over four days with 91% turnout and passed, remarkably, peacefully given the violence that preceded it. Historian Tom Lodge's explanation for this outcome — changed perceptions, changed white thinking, violence proving compromise necessary, both sides retaining control of their own armed forces, and capable leadership on both sides — is best understood through Sources R and U together: the transition satisfied enough of the expectation in Source R, and contained enough of the rejection in Source U, that neither destroyed the settlement.

questions.questionHtml: Evaluate the effectiveness of international responses in bringing about the end of apartheid. In your answer, refer to Source R.
questions.planHtml:
Introduction — Thesis

International responses to apartheid were largely symbolic, and therefore only marginally effective, for around twenty-five years; they became decisive only once they became economic, because the apartheid state could survive being condemned but not being made unaffordable.

Body Paragraph 1 — Source R and the symbolic campaign

Source R, a Free Nelson Mandela poster published in Washington D.C. in 1988 — the same year the Wembley concert drew 92,000 people and a global BBC broadcast — is evidence of an international campaign that had been building since Tambo launched it in 1980 and had gathered a petition of 20,000 mayors' names. That the South African government made it a crime to carry or promote Mandela's image is itself a measure of how much the campaign unsettled the regime; but Source R is a poster, not a sanction, and shows public pressure rather than the mechanism that actually forced change.

Body Paragraph 2 — early responses had limited effect

The UN Security Council passed Resolution 134 within eleven days of Sharpeville in 1960, condemning the massacre, yet foreign investors returned to South Africa within a short time, still drawn by cheap labour — showing that condemnation without economic cost changed very little in the earlier period.

Body Paragraph 3 — responses became decisive once they were economic

By contrast, the sanctions and disinvestment campaigns of the mid-1980s had a measurable economic effect: US investment in South Africa fell by around 40% after the 1986 sanctions law, and roughly 250 international companies withdrew from South Africa by 1987. Combined with the cost of Total Strategy and cross-border military operations, this contributed to a 1985 debt crisis, a 35% depreciation of the Rand, and growth of only around 1.5% by 1989 — pressure severe enough to affect white South Africans' confidence, including that of a future president, de Klerk, that apartheid could still protect their own economic interests.

Conclusion — Judgement

Judged across the full period, international responses to apartheid were consistently vocal but not consistently effective — Source R captures the campaign at its most visible, in 1988, yet the shift from condemnation to compliance came only once measures like the 1986 sanctions law and mass disinvestment made apartheid economically unsustainable, confirming that effectiveness tracked economic cost far more closely than moral outrage.

questions.questionHtml: Explain why the Pan-Africanist Congress (PAC) broke away from the ANC in 1959, and how this shaped the organisation of the anti-pass campaign that led to Sharpeville.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Robert Sobukwe led a breakaway from the ANC in 1959, rejecting the multiracial approach of the 1955 Freedom Charter in favour of a more explicitly Africanist, Africa-for-Africans platform.
  • To assert leadership through direct action, the PAC organised its own anti-pass campaign for 21 March 1960 — deliberately ahead of a planned ANC campaign — leading directly to the gathering at Sharpeville.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the extent to which internal resistance to apartheid between 1960 and 1976 was shaped more by underground organisation than by mass public protest.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • After the 1960 bannings, the ANC and PAC operated mainly underground and in exile — Umkhonto we Sizwe's sabotage campaign (from 1961) and the Rivonia Trial (1963–64) reflect this clandestine phase.
  • By contrast, the Black Consciousness Movement from 1968–69 rebuilt a form of open, public organisation (SASO, BPC) that operated legally until banned in 1977.
  • Judgement: the period splits roughly in two — underground/exile organisation dominated the early-to-mid 1960s, while open (if closely watched) public organisation returned with Black Consciousness from the end of the decade, feeding into the mass protest of 1976.

groups.title: Repression, Bantustans & the End of Apartheid

questions.questionHtml: Explain how the South African government used legal and security measures to repress opposition in the 1980s.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • Legal basis: the General Law Amendment Act (1963) allowed 90-day detention without charge, later extended indefinitely at the Minister of Justice's discretion with no judicial review.
  • "Total Strategy": Botha framed resistance as a "total onslaught", justifying military-style rule — sequential States of Emergency from 1985 gave security forces sweeping detention and censorship powers.
  • Security forces: the merged police/SADF and covert units such as Koevoet used mass detention (around 30,000 by 1988), torture and deaths in custody, including Steve Biko's in 1977.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the significance of the Bantustan policy as a method of controlling Black South Africans.
questions.planHtml:
Thesis

The Bantustan policy was significant less as a genuine attempt at self-government than as a tool for fragmenting Black political identity and formally stripping Black South Africans of citizenship — its practical failure as an economic or diplomatic project does not diminish how effectively it served this narrower political goal.

Point 1 — legal mechanism

The 1970 Black Homelands Citizenship Act reassigned Black South Africans' citizenship to a Bantustan regardless of where they actually lived, formally excising millions of people from any political claim on South Africa itself.

Point 2 — fragmentation strategy

Dividing Black South Africans along ten ethnic lines was intended to encourage separate ethnic identities over a unified Black political consciousness, directly undercutting movements like the ANC that organised across ethnic lines.

Point 3 — practical failure

The four Bantustans granted "independence" from 1976 were recognised by no country besides South Africa, held about 13% of the land for a much larger share of the population, and remained economically dependent on South Africa — undermining the claim they represented genuine self-determination.

Judgement

Judged as nation-building, the policy failed completely; judged as a tool of political control and citizenship removal, it succeeded exactly as intended — which is the more accurate way to assess its significance.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the significance of economic factors in bringing about the end of apartheid.
questions.planHtml:
Key points to include (with evidence)
  • International sanctions and disinvestment reduced US investment in South Africa by around 40% within four years of the 1986 US sanctions law.
  • A 1985 debt crisis forced the temporary closure of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and a 35% depreciation of the Rand.
  • Combined with heavy military spending on "Total Strategy", economic growth fell to around 1.5% by early 1989 — eroding white South Africans' confidence that apartheid could still protect their interests.
